MUJAHID:v1p320#3/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p320#3/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v1p320#3/r1.claim: Mujahid says Jacob feared his family would accuse him of losing his mind.

MUQATIL:12:91-95/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:12:91-95/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:12:91-95/r4.claim: The caravan traveled eighty farsakhs from Egypt toward Canaan when Jacob smelled Joseph's scent; “foolish” means treating him as senile or ignorant.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p328#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p328#2/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p328#2/r1.claim: Qatada glosses تفندون as calling someone foolish or senile.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p329/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p329/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p329/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says a wind carried Joseph's shirt scent to Jacob when the caravan departed; Jacob could smell it from eight days away.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p222#4/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p222#4/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p222#4/r1.claim: Tufannidūn means incapacitate me; it can also mean accuse me of foolishness or ignorance, as old age can muddle speech.

TAB-FULL:v13p332/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p332/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p332/r1.claim: As Jacob’s sons’ caravan departed from Joseph toward him, Jacob said that he could smell Joseph.

TAB-FULL:v13p332/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p332/r2.speaker: أبو أيوب الهوزني
TAB-FULL:v13p332/r2.claim: Abu Ayyub al-Hawzani reports that the wind asked God to carry Joseph’s scent to Jacob before the herald arrived, and God permitted it.

TAB-FULL:v13p332/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p332/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v13p332/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says a wind carried the scent of Joseph’s shirt from eight nights away; another report gives seven or eight nights and compares the distance to Basra–Kufa.

TAB-FULL:v13p334/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p334/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v13p334/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas estimates the scent traveled from the distance between Basra and Kufa, or eight nights, and identifies it as the scent of Joseph’s shirt.

TAB-FULL:v13p334/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p334/r2.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v13p334/r2.claim: Al-Hasan says Joseph and Jacob were eighty parasangs apart at the time, Joseph in Egypt and Jacob in Canaan.

TAB-FULL:v13p334/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p334/r3.speaker: ابن جريج
TAB-FULL:v13p334/r3.claim: Ibn Jurayj reports a distance of eighty parasangs and says Joseph had been separated from Jacob for seventy-seven years.

TAB-FULL:v13p336/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p336/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v13p336/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas repeatedly says the wind carried the scent of Joseph’s shirt to Jacob from eight days away.

TAB-FULL:v13p336/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p336/r2.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v13p336/r2.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Jacob sensed Joseph’s scent when the caravan left Egypt.

TAB-FULL:v13p336/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p336/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p336/r3.claim: تفندون means scold, accuse of incapacity, blame, or call a speaker a liar; أفنده الدهر means age impaired him, as poetry illustrates الإفناد.

TAB-FULL:v13p336/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p336/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v13p336/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses تفندون as calling Jacob foolish.

TAB-FULL:v13p336/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p336/r5.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v13p336/r5.claim: Mujahid likewise glosses تفندون as calling Jacob foolish.

TAB-FULL:v13p338/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p338/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v13p338/r1.claim: Reports from Ibn Abbas and Sa‘id differ: one glosses the phrase as calling Jacob foolish, the other as calling him a liar.

TAB-FULL:v13p338/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p338/r2.speaker: عطاء
TAB-FULL:v13p338/r2.claim: Ata says the phrase means “unless you call me a liar” or “unless you deem me foolish.”

TAB-FULL:v13p338/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p338/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v13p338/r3.claim: Qatada glosses it as “unless you deem me foolish.”

TAB-FULL:v13p338/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p338/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v13p338/r4.claim: Mujahid explains it as “unless you say my mind is gone.”

TAB-FULL:v13p338/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p338/r5.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v13p338/r5.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Jacob feared that his family would weaken or discredit him.

TAB-FULL:v13p339/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p339/r1.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v13p339/r1.claim: Ibn Zayd describes a person who lacks reason as mufannad, explaining the sense of being called irrational.

TAB-FULL:v13p339/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p339/r2.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v13p339/r2.claim: Al-Suddi and several other authorities gloss تفندون as accusing Jacob of lying.

TAB-FULL:v13p339/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p339/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v13p339/r3.claim: Mujahid also reports the gloss “unless you grow old,” alongside his other reported senses.

TAB-FULL:v13p339/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p339/r4.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v13p339/r4.claim: Al-Hasan interprets تفندون as “unless you grow old.”

TAB-FULL:v13p339/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p339/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p339/r5.claim: Al-Tabari reconciles the reported meanings because tafnīd fundamentally denotes corruption: bodily corruption includes old age, lost reason, and weakness, while acts include lying and false blame.

TAB-FULL:v13p341/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p341/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p341/r1.claim: A cited poem uses tafnīd for blame; al-Tabari concludes the reported interpretations are close, all fit the verse, and none is uniquely established by its wording.

ZAJJAJ:v3p128/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p128/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p128/r4.claim: Lāw lā an tufannidūn means ‘if only you did not call me ignorant’; another report reads it as accusing him of foolishness.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r2.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r2.claim: The caravan departed Egypt for Syria.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r3.claim: Jacob smelled Joseph's shirt from a distance of eight nights' travel.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r4.claim: Another report puts the distance at six days' travel.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r5.claim: Another report gives the distance as ten days.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r6.claim: Another report places the scent eighty parasangs away, approximately the distance between Basra and Kufa.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r7.claim: “Tufannidūn” means that you call me foolish; Ata is also reported to give this interpretation.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r8.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2197/r8.claim: Another interpretation of “tufannidūn” is “if you call me a liar.”

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2198/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2198/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2198/r1.claim: The phrase means “if you do not think me old and feeble.”

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2198/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2198/r2.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن اسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2198/r2.claim: A person without reason is called “mufannad”; the poet's line “gently, for among minds is one made foolish” witnesses to the word.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v5p255#2/r1.claim: Mujahid glosses لولا أن تفندون as fearing that others will deem Jacob's judgment foolish.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r10.speaker: الكسائي
THALABI:v5p255#2/r10.claim: Al-Kisa'i interprets the word as incapacity or inability.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r11.speaker: الأخفش
THALABI:v5p255#2/r11.claim: Al-Akhfash says it means blaming Jacob.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r12.speaker: أبو عبيدة
THALABI:v5p255#2/r12.claim: Abu Ubayda glosses it as leading Jacob astray or deeming him deluded.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r13.speaker: النابغة
THALABI:v5p255#2/r13.claim: Al-Nabigha uses الفند for corruption, supporting the word's root sense.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r14.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p255#2/r14.claim: The root sense of الفند is corruption; blame is called tafnid, and the source cites several poems for that usage.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r15.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r15.speaker: جرير بن عطية
THALABI:v5p255#2/r15.claim: Jarir's verse uses التفنيد for reproach or blame.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r16.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r16.speaker: ابن مقبل
THALABI:v5p255#2/r16.claim: Ibn Muqbil uses الإفناد for the corruption caused by time.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r17.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r17.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p255#2/r17.claim: The sons of Jacob are meant by قالوا, and they accuse their father of his old error: continued love for Yusuf.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r18.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r18.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v5p255#2/r18.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the bearer of glad tidings as Judah, Jacob's son.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r19.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r19.speaker: ابن مسعود
THALABI:v5p255#2/r19.claim: Ibn Masud says the messenger arrived from the front of the caravan.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v5p255#2/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the phrase as fearing they will consider him ignorant.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r20.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r20.speaker: السدي
THALABI:v5p255#2/r20.claim: Al-Suddi says Judah volunteered to carry the shirt because he had previously taken the bloody shirt to Jacob and now wanted to bring him joy.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r21.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r21.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v5p255#2/r21.claim: Ibn Abbas says Judah carried the shirt alone, ran barefoot and bareheaded, and covered eighty farsakhs with seven loaves still uneaten.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r22.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r22.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v5p255#2/r22.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits from Ibn Abbas that the bearer was Malik ibn Dhuar from Midian.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r23.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r23.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p255#2/r23.claim: ألقاه means the messenger laid Yusuf's shirt on Jacob's face, and ارتد بصيرا means he regained sight after blindness.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r3.speaker: ابن جريج
THALABI:v5p255#2/r3.claim: Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Abi Najih report Mujahid's gloss: unless they say Jacob has lost his mind.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r4.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
THALABI:v5p255#2/r4.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, and al-Dahhak say it means unless they call Jacob a liar; al-Awfi also transmits that gloss from Ibn Abbas.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r5.speaker: الحسن
THALABI:v5p255#2/r5.claim: Al-Hasan and Qatada interpret تفندون as growing old; another report from Mujahid gives the same sense.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r6.speaker: ربيع
THALABI:v5p255#2/r6.claim: Rabi glosses it as being called foolish or mad.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r7.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v5p255#2/r7.claim: Juwaybir's report from al-Dahhak explains the phrase as fearing they will say Jacob is senile and has lost his reason.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r8.speaker: ابن يسار
THALABI:v5p255#2/r8.claim: Ibn Yasar says it means they will weaken or find Jacob feeble.

THALABI:v5p255#2/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255#2/r9.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء
THALABI:v5p255#2/r9.claim: Abu Amr ibn al-Ala glosses it as finding Jacob disgraceful.

THALABI:v5p255/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p255/r1.claim: The caravan set out from Arish in Egypt toward Canaan.

THALABI:v5p255/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p255/r2.claim: A report says the wind asked God to carry Yusuf's scent to Jacob before the messenger arrived; God allowed it, and the wind carried the shirt's scent.

THALABI:v5p255/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255/r3.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v5p255/r3.claim: A report through al-Suddi from his father from Mujahid says Jacob sensed Yusuf's scent from a distance of three days.

THALABI:v5p255/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v5p255/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says Jacob detected Yusuf's scent from eight nights away.

THALABI:v5p255/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v5p255/r5.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas places the scent's distance between Basra and Kufa.

THALABI:v5p255/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p255/r6.speaker: الحسن
THALABI:v5p255/r6.claim: Al-Hasan reports that the distance between Jacob and Yusuf was eighty farsakhs.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r10.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r10.claim: Ja'far ibn Muhammad identifies the breeze as the east wind.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r11.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r11.claim: لولا أن تفندون means unless you call me foolish or senile.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r7.claim: The caravan had departed Egypt and was heading toward Syria.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r8.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r8.claim: Jacob may have sensed signs and indications that made his expectation strong; the expression comes from sensing an approaching scent or sign.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p76/r9.claim: The majority say Jacob smelled Joseph's familiar scent itself.

QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r10.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r10.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r10.claim: Only Jacob sensed Joseph because he alone grieved over his loss; only those who love the beloved recognize the beloved’s fragrance.

QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r11.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r11.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r11.claim: The word scent is also used figuratively, as in saying someone’s influence blows or that one senses the scent of discord.

QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r12.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r12.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r12.claim: Jacob anticipated blame, but his sons answered with increasingly insulting reproaches and called his loving devotion delusion.

QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r8.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r8.claim: While hardship continued, Joseph’s story remained obscure to Jacob; once the trial lifted, his state became apparent.

QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p91/r9.claim: Joseph had not been physically far away when thrown into the well, but his identity and condition were obscured; Jacob sensed him from eighty farsakhs away.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r1.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r1.claim: فصل can mean departing from someone or sending a letter; it is intransitive or transitive, with different verbal nouns for the two uses.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r2.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r2.claim: When the caravan left Egypt for Canaan, Jacob told the relatives present that he could smell Joseph; his sons were absent.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r3.claim: In Ibn Abī al-Hudhayl's report, wind carried Joseph's shirt scent to Jacob from a distance of eight nights' travel.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r4.speaker: الحسن
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r4.claim: Al-Ḥasan says Jacob smelled Joseph from ten days' travel away.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r5.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r5.claim: Qatāda says they reported a distance of eighty farsakhs between them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r6.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r6.claim: Mujāhid explains that wind fluttered the shirt and carried the scent of Paradise into the world to Jacob, who knew the shirt bore that fragrance.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r7.speaker: أهل المعاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r7.claim: God let Jacob smell Joseph as the trial ended and relief came from far away, while withholding the scent when Joseph was nearby in the well and when sold, to test him and perfect his reward.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p242/r8.claim: أجد ريح يوسف means “I smell Joseph's scent”; it is expressed as finding because smelling is a form of perception.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r1.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r1.claim: تفندون can mean that a man has become senile or lost his reason, or has become ignorant and is attributed to foolishness.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r10.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r10.claim: Muḥammad b. Isḥāq interprets it as “unless you deem me weak.”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r11.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r11.claim: These interpretations derive from الفند, meaning foolishness or ignorance, as in al-Nābigha's line.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r2.speaker: الليث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r2.claim: Al-Layth defines الفند as loss of reason in old age; an old man with this condition is called شيخ مفند.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r3.speaker: الأصمعي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r3.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī says a person who rambles at length from senility is called مفند.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r4.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r4.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī says فند رأيه means to weaken or discredit someone's judgment.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r5.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r5.claim: Al-Farrāʾ interprets لولا أن تفندون as “unless you call me a liar, defeat me, or weaken me.”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r6.speaker: أبو عبيد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r6.claim: Abū ʿUbayd interprets it as “unless you call me foolish.”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r7.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r7.claim: Al-Zajjāj interprets it as “unless you consider me ignorant.”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets it as “unless you call me a liar.”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r9.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p243/r9.claim: Mujāhid takes it as “unless you consider me foolish and say I have lost my mind.”

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:94-96/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:94-96/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:94-96/r1.claim: The caravan left Egypt for Canaan; a wind carried the scent of Joseph's shirt to Jacob, who recognized the scent of Paradise.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:94-96/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:94-96/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:94-96/r2.claim: Jacob knew that the shirt's scent was from Paradise because no other scent of Paradise existed on earth.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:94-96/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:94-96/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:94-96/r3.claim: “Unless you think me senile” means unless you regard Jacob as foolish or ignorant.

JISHUMI:v5p3713/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r1.claim: He recited that the bearer came from in front of the caravan; the author treats this as explanatory wording, not Qurʾān.

JISHUMI:v5p3713/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r10.speaker: الحسن والأصم
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r10.claim: They give the scent's travel time as a month's journey.

JISHUMI:v5p3713/r11.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r11.speaker: الحسن
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r11.claim: He also gives the distance as eighty farsakhs.

JISHUMI:v5p3713/r12.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r12.speaker: مجاهد
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r12.claim: He says the scent reached Jacob from a three-day journey away.

JISHUMI:v5p3713/r13.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r13.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r13.claim: God conveyed the scent as a miracle so Jacob would know Joseph's hardship had ended, receive comfort, and anticipate reunion and his son's life.

JISHUMI:v5p3713/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r2.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r2.claim: Faṣl means cutting or separating, and a judge is called a fāṣil because he settles matters; its opposite is joining.

JISHUMI:v5p3713/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r3.claim: Tafnīd is weakening someone's judgment; it can also mean corruption, as in the cited poetry and usage.

JISHUMI:v5p3713/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r7.claim: The caravan had left Egypt for Canaan; Jacob speaks to his grandsons because his sons were still in Egypt with the caravan.

JISHUMI:v5p3713/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r8.speaker: مفسرون
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r8.claim: On the literal reading, Jacob smelled Joseph's actual scent carried by the air; commentators disagree over how far it traveled.

JISHUMI:v5p3713/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
JISHUMI:v5p3713/r9.claim: He says the wind brought Joseph's scent from a distance of eight nights.

JISHUMI:v5p3715/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r1.speaker: أبو مسلم
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r1.claim: Alternatively, Jacob had strong hope or revelation about Joseph and the brothers, and used scent metaphorically, as in speaking of the scent of good; the author also allows the literal view.

JISHUMI:v5p3715/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r2.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r2.claim: They explain lولا أن تفندون as ‘lest you call me a liar.’

JISHUMI:v5p3715/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r3.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r3.claim: They explain it as ‘lest you think me senile.’

JISHUMI:v5p3715/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r4.speaker: ابن إسحاق
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r4.claim: He explains the phrase as ‘lest you weaken me.’

JISHUMI:v5p3715/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r5.speaker: الأخفش وأبو مسلم
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r5.claim: They understand the phrase as ‘lest you reproach me.’

JISHUMI:v5p3715/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r6.speaker: أبو عبيدة
JISHUMI:v5p3715/r6.claim: He explains the phrase as ‘lest you lead me astray.’

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r1.claim: The caravan had left the Egyptian town of Arish for Canaan when Jacob spoke to his grandchildren about smelling Joseph.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r2.claim: A report says the east wind asked God’s permission to bring Jacob Joseph’s scent before the bearer arrived.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r3.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r3.claim: Mujahid says Jacob smelled Joseph from three days’ travel away; Ibn Abbas says eight nights, while al-Hasan says eighty farsakhs.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r4.claim: Another view says a wind carried the shirt’s scent to Jacob; he recognized the scent of Paradise, which could only be on earth in that garment.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p275/r5.claim: تفندون means calling him foolish; Ibn Abbas says treating him as ignorant, al-Dahhak says calling him senile, others say weakening him, and Abu Ubayda says misleading him; the root means corruption.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r1.claim: The caravan separated from Egypt's outskirts and passed its walls; Ibn ʿAbbās reads fa-lammā infaṣala al-ʿīr, when the caravan departed.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase as when the caravan separated and departed.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r3.claim: God enabled Jacob to smell Joseph's shirt as it approached from a journey of eight days; he speaks to his grandchildren and those around him.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r4.claim: Tufannidūn means accusing someone of senility or impaired reason; only a man is called mufannad because he had judgment in youth to lose in old age.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p475/r5.claim: Jacob means that without their calling him senile, they would believe his report; their old error was excessive love, constant mention, and hope of reunion with Joseph, whom they thought dead.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r10.speaker: أبو أيوب الهوزني
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r10.claim: Abu Ayyub al-Hawzani reports that the wind asked permission to carry Joseph’s scent to Jacob and was permitted.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r11.claim: Jacob addressed people around him who were variously said to be his grandchildren, some of his sons, or relatives.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r6.claim: Jacob’s home is identified either near Jerusalem or in al-Jazira; the author prefers near Jerusalem because their traces and graves are there.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas says Joseph’s scent reached Jacob across an eight-day journey when a wind carried it.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r8.speaker: الحسن وابن جريج
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r8.claim: Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj give the distance as eighty farsakhs; Ibn Jurayj says Joseph had been gone for seventy-seven years.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r9.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p278#2/r9.claim: Another report from al-Hasan gives the distance as a thirty-day journey; the author considers this close to Ibn Abbas’s account.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r1.claim: Tufannidūn means to reject Jacob’s judgment or argue back; afsada al-dahr means that time ruined someone.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r10.speaker: الطبري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r10.claim: Al-Tabari says the root sense of fanad is corruption.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r2.claim: Poets use fanad for ruin and decay; al-Mundhir ibn Saʿid says a man can be described as an old fool but not a woman.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r3.claim: People may accuse someone of fanad because of ignorance, overpowering desire, lying, or weakness and mental decline.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r4.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada say the brothers meant that Jacob was foolish; Ibn Abbas also glosses it as ignorance.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r5.speaker: ابن جبير وعطاء
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r5.claim: Ibn Jubayr and ʿAtaʾ interpret the phrase as accusing Jacob of lying.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r6.speaker: ابن إسحاق
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r6.claim: Ibn Ishaq says the brothers meant that Jacob had become weak.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r7.speaker: ابن زيد ومجاهد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r7.claim: Ibn Zayd and Mujahid say the brothers meant to accuse Jacob of having lost his mind.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r8.speaker: الحسن
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r8.claim: Al-Hasan interprets the phrase as saying that Jacob had grown old.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p279/r9.claim: The author thinks the brothers accused Jacob because they believed his love for Joseph had overpowered his judgment.

TABRISI:12:94-96/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:94-96/r1.speaker: ابن عباس، مجاهد
TABRISI:12:94-96/r1.claim: Lāwlā an tufannidūn means 'if only you would not call me foolish,' according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

TABRISI:12:94-96/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:94-96/r2.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TABRISI:12:94-96/r2.claim: Ibn Ishaq interprets it as 'if only you would not weaken my judgment.'

TABRISI:12:94-96/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:94-96/r3.speaker: سعيد بن جبير، السدي، الضحاك، الحسن، قتادة
TABRISI:12:94-96/r3.claim: Other explanations are 'call me a liar' or 'say I am old, senile, and have lost my mind'; Ibn Abbas is also reported with the liar interpretation.

TABRISI:12:94-96/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:94-96/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:94-96/r4.claim: Jacob means that he is certain the scent is Yusuf's; the other readings describe what he fears his sons will say.

TABRISI:12:94/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:94/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:94/r1.claim: Faṣl means separation or cutting; a judge is called faṣīl because he settles and cuts through disputes.

TABRISI:12:94/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:94/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:94/r2.claim: Tafnīd means weakening someone's judgment; another derivation calls it corruption, supported by poetry.

TABRISI:12:94/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:94/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:94/r3.claim: When the caravan left Egypt and headed toward Syria, Jacob told his descendants with him that he could smell Yusuf.

TABRISI:12:94/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:94/r4.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABRISI:12:94/r4.claim: Abu ʿAbd Allah reports that Jacob smelled Yusuf's shirt as the caravan departed from ten days' distance in Palestine; other estimates are eight nights, eighty farsakhs, or a month's journey.

TABRISI:12:94/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:94/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:12:94/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says a wind carried the scent of Yusuf's shirt to Jacob; a story says the east wind sought and received permission to bring it before the bearer arrived.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r1.claim: The caravan departed Egypt for Canaan; Judah carried Joseph's shirt and said he had brought Jacob the false bloody shirt that grieved him, so now he would carry good news.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says Judah set off barefoot and bareheaded, running with seven loaves he had not finished eating.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r3.claim: “Their father” means Jacob addressing his present family, relatives, and grandchildren; “I find” means “I smell.”

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r4.claim: The accompanying poetic lines show that wajada is used for sensing a scent.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r5.claim: One answer to why Jacob smelled Joseph from far away but not nearer before is that God concealed Joseph's affair until the trial and reward were complete.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r6.speaker: مجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r6.claim: Mujahid says spreading the heavenly shirt released Paradise's scent; a wind carried it to Jacob, who knew it came from the shirt.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r7.claim: A report says the east wind asked permission to carry Joseph's scent to Jacob before the herald arrived; it was granted, and the soft wind consoles the sorrowful.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r8.speaker: أبو صخر الهذلي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r8.claim: Abu Sakhr al-Hudhali's verse describes the east wind from the direction of dawn reviving sorrow.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p283#2/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas estimates that Jacob smelled Joseph's shirt from eight nights' journey, or eighty farsakhs.

RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r1.claim: Faṣala can mean to depart intransitively, with maṣdar fuṣūl, or to send something, with maṣdar faṣl; Jacob's caravan was leaving Egypt for Canaan.

RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r2.claim: Jacob addressed his household and relatives, not his sons, who were away; this follows from his later telling them to go and seek Joseph.

RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r3.claim: The distance between Jacob and the caravan is variously estimated as eight days, ten days, or eighty farsakhs.

RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r4.claim: Mujahid says a wind carried the shirt, spreading the scent of Paradise through the world to Jacob, who knew that its fragrance could only come from that shirt.

RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r5.speaker: أنس بن مالك
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r5.claim: A report transmitted by al-Wahidi from Anas and the Prophet says Gabriel brought Abraham a heavenly shirt and rug in Nimrod's fire; the shirt passed through Isaac and Jacob to Joseph, who kept it in a silver case.

RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r6.claim: Al-Razi says the decisive explanation is a miracle: God conveyed Joseph's scent over an extraordinary distance, most likely as a sign for Jacob, who had been mocked for his claim.

RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p165#2/r7.claim: The miracle shows that during hardship even an easy thing can become difficult, while in a favorable time a difficult thing becomes easy; Jacob had lacked news of nearby Joseph for eighty years yet now smelled him from far away.

RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r1.claim: Jacob says he smells Joseph; he describes the olfactory perception as finding because smell is a sense by which something is found.

RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r2.speaker: أبو بكر ابن الأنباري
RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r2.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says afnada can mean grief altered a person's reason, while fannada can mean attributing ignorance to him.

RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r3.speaker: الأصمعي
RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r3.claim: Al-Asma'i says a man whose speech becomes excessive from senility is called mufannad.

RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r4.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r4.claim: Al-Kashshaf says one says shaykh mufannad but not عجوز مفندة, since she had no sound judgment in youth to lose in old age.

RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p166/r5.claim: Jacob means: if you did not accuse me of senility, when he says he smells Joseph.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r1.claim: The caravan departed from Egypt toward Syria; faṣala can be intransitive or transitive, and the father speaks to relatives who stayed behind, perhaps grandchildren, though some sons may have traveled.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r10.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r10.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī, also followed by Ibn Isḥāq, takes it as weakening Jacob's opinion; fand is impaired judgment in old age.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r11.speaker: أبو عبيدة
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r11.claim: Abū ʿUbayda glosses the phrase as misleading Jacob.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r12.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r12.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Mujāhid also interpret it as saying Jacob has grown old; these related explanations return to incapacitating and weakening judgment, including mistaken speech.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says a wind carried Joseph's shirt scent to Jacob across eight nights of travel.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r3.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r3.claim: Al-Ḥasan estimates the distance at ten nights in one report and one month in another.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r4.speaker: مالك بن أنس
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r4.claim: Mālik ibn Anas says the shirt's scent reached Jacob by a means like the transport of Bilqīs's throne to Solomon before his glance returned.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r5.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r5.claim: Mujāhid says wind fluttered the shirt and brought the fragrance of Paradise into the world to Jacob; he knew the scent could only come from that shirt.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r6.claim: The phrase innī li-ajidu means I smell, a finding through the sense of smell.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid interpret tufannidūn as calling Jacob foolish, supported by al-Nābigha's use of fand for foolishness.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r8.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r8.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk interpret the phrase as accusing Jacob of lying; fand means falsehood, supported by a poetic use of fand.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r9.speaker: أبو عمرو
QURTUBI-FULL:12:94/r9.claim: Abū ʿAmr explains it as condemning Jacob or disparaging his judgment; a poet uses tafnīd for blame.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r1.claim: The caravan leaves Egypt and its settled area; Jacob says this to those around him.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r2.claim: God made Joseph's scent carried on the shirt reach Jacob through Judah from a distance of eighty farsakhs.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r3.claim: To accuse Jacob of tafnīd is to attribute age-related mental decline to him; the term is not used for an old woman because her deficiency is innate.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:94/r4.claim: The answer to the conditional is omitted: Jacob would have been believed, or would have said Joseph was near.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p204#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p204#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p204#2/r1.claim: The caravan departed from Arish in Egypt; faṣala means leaving a town and passing beyond its walls.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p204#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p204#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p204#2/r2.claim: Joseph's scent reached Jacob by God's enabling him to smell the shirt from a journey of eight days.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p204#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p204#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p204#2/r3.claim: Tafnīd means attributing fand, grief, or impaired reason from old age; Jacob says they would believe him if they did not accuse him of that.

QASHANI:12:93-98/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:93-98/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:93-98/r4.claim: Jacob's sensing the scent from afar means the heart's return affects intellect and reason and directs animal faculties to lawful, just appetites; the caravan is beautifully equipped.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r10.claim: Lājad means perceiving by smell; a poem illustrates detecting a breeze from the beloved’s land.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r11.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r11.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada gloss tufannidūn as calling Jacob foolish.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r12.speaker: عطاء وابن جبير
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r12.claim: ʿAta and Ibn Jubayr interpret the word as accusing Jacob of lying.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r13.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r13.claim: Al-Hasan offers ‘you consider me aged’ as another meaning.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r5.claim: Faṣala can mean depart intransitively or separate something transitively; here the caravan set out from Egypt toward Jacob.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas’s reading says the caravan separated; he says Jacob detected Joseph’s scent from eight days away as wind carried it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r7.speaker: الحسن وابن جريج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r7.claim: Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj estimate the scent traveled eighty farsakhs; other reports from al-Hasan say thirty days or ten nights, with separation lasting seventy-seven years.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r8.speaker: أبو أيوب المهروي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r8.claim: Abu Ayyub al-Mahwuri says the wind asked permission to carry Joseph’s scent to Jacob, and permission was granted.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r9.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p322#2/r9.claim: Mujahid says the wind flapped the shirt, spreading the scent of paradise until Jacob recognized it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r1.speaker: ابن زيد والضحاك ومجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r1.claim: Ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak, and Mujahid gloss it as saying Jacob had lost his mind or become senile; other views say disparage, incapacitate, mislead, or accuse him of error.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r2.claim: These glosses converge on judging the speaker’s view unsound, from ignorance, bias, falsehood, weakness, or old age.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r3.speaker: منذر بن سعيد البلوطي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r3.claim: Munthir ibn Saʿid says shaykh mufannad describes a corrupted judgment, but an old woman is not called mufannadah because she never had an established opinion to lose.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r4.claim: Al-Zamakhshari derives tafnīd from old age, fear, and loss of reason, likewise avoiding its use for a woman.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies the omitted result of lawlā as ‘you would have believed me if you did not undermine me.’

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r6.claim: The author instead proposes that without their accusation Jacob would have told them that the scent showed Joseph was alive.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p323/r7.claim: The addressees are most likely children left at home, though they could be grandchildren and other relatives.

SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r1.claim: تفندون means corrupt someone's judgment or rebut his opinion; the cited poem uses تفنيدي in this sense.

SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r2.claim: أفند الدهر فلانا means age corrupted him; the cited verse uses الإفناد.

SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r3.speaker: النابغة
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r3.claim: Al-Nabigha uses الفند for corruption or error in his verse about Solomon.

SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r4.claim: الفند also means a mountain spur; it became a man's name, and al-Fand al-Zamani is a Hamasa poet.

SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says شيخ مفند is idiomatic but عجوز مفندة is not, claiming an old woman had no youthful judgment to corrupt; the author calls this odd.

SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:94/r6.claim: The جواب of counterfactual لولا is omitted; proposed completions are “you would believe me” or “I would tell you.”

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata, Qatada, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explain 'you would deem me foolish' as accusing Jacob of folly or infantilizing him.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409#2/r2.claim: Mujahid and al-Hasan also explain the phrase as saying Jacob had grown senile.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409/r2.claim: As the caravan left Egypt, Jacob told the sons remaining with him that he could smell Yusuf, fearing they would call him senile.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says a wind carried the scent of Yusuf's shirt to Jacob when the caravan departed, and Jacob detected it from eight days' distance; al-Thawri and Shu'ba transmit the report too.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409/r4.speaker: الحسن
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p409/r4.claim: Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj say Jacob and Yusuf were eighty parasangs apart and had been separated for eighty years.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p95/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p95/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p95/r4.claim: The caravan had left al-ʿArīsh, the last Egyptian town toward Syria, when Jacob strongly affirmed that he could smell Joseph’s scent.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p95/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p95/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p95/r5.claim: Jacob’s “if you did not think me senile” means he is stating his perception despite expecting disbelief; tafnīd is accusing an old person of failing judgment.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p95/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p95/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p95/r6.claim: Biqāʿī explains fasalat as leaving a place, wijdān as perception that rules out nonexistence, and scent as what the nose detects.

DURR-FULL:v4p508/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p508/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v4p508/r1.claim: As the caravan departed for Syria, Jacob sensed Joseph's scent and told his descendants; they accused him of remaining in his old error about Joseph.

DURR-FULL:v4p580/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p580/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v4p580/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas relates that a shirt passed from paradise through Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to Joseph; as Jacob received its scent from eight stages away, the report says no heavenly thing touches a worldly ailment without healing it by God's permission.

DURR-FULL:v4p580/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p580/r2.speaker: المطلب بن عبد الله بن حنطب
DURR-FULL:v4p580/r2.claim: A second account says the shirt was placed in a silver tube around Joseph's neck when he was thrown in the well, imprisoned, and visited by his brothers; Jacob smelled it in Canaan when it was sent to him.

DURR-FULL:v4p580/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p580/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v4p580/r3.claim: Ibn Masud says Jacob's family numbered ninety-three when they arrived in Egypt; they later left with Moses as 670,000 people.

DURR-FULL:v4p580/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p580/r4.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
DURR-FULL:v4p580/r4.claim: Al-Rabiʿ says Jacob traveled to Egypt with seventy-two descendants and his family later left with Moses as six hundred thousand.

DURR-FULL:v4p580/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p580/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v4p580/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says the departing caravan stirred a wind that carried Joseph's shirt scent to Jacob, who feared his family would call him foolish.

DURR-FULL:v4p581/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p581/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v4p581/r1.claim: Reports from Ibn Abbas give different distances for Jacob smelling Joseph's shirt: eight days, ten days, eighty farsakhs, and six days; Hasan says a month, and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb seven days.

DURR-FULL:v4p581/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p581/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v4p581/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses lولا أن تفندون as lest you deem me ignorant; another report says lest you accuse me of lying.

DURR-FULL:v4p581/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p581/r3.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v4p581/r3.claim: Mujahid says Jacob feared that his family would call him old and claim that his mind had gone.

DURR-FULL:v4p581/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p581/r4.speaker: ابن زيد
DURR-FULL:v4p581/r4.claim: Ibn Zayd says a mufannad is someone without reason and cites a poem in which the word mufannad witnesses this meaning.

DURR-FULL:v4p581/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p581/r5.speaker: الربيع
DURR-FULL:v4p581/r5.claim: Al-Rabiʿ glosses the phrase as lest you call me foolish.

BURSEVI:v4p206#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p206#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p206#2/r1.claim: The Sufi anecdotes treat fragrance as a spiritual sign beyond ordinary sight: Bayazid sensed Abu al-Hasan al-Kharqani’s coming presence, as the Prophet sensed a divine fragrance from Yemen and Uways al-Qarani.

BURSEVI:v4p206#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p206#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p206#2/r2.claim: Fand means senility, impaired reason, and corrupt judgment caused by old age; one calls an old man mufannad, not an old woman, whose poor judgment is not newly caused by age.

BURSEVI:v4p206#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p206#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p206#2/r3.claim: The unspoken result of ‘were it not that you would accuse me’ is that they would believe him; senility does not afflict prophets and spiritual heirs.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r1.claim: The caravan leaves from the town of al-Arish in Egypt toward Jacob, who is near Jerusalem; the claim that Jacob lived in al-Jazira is not reliable.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r2.claim: Intransitive فصل means to depart a town and cross its walls, while transitive فصل means to separate something; Ibn Abbas reads انفصل العير.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas reads ولما انفصل العير, 'when the caravan separated/departed'.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r4.claim: Jacob says he smells Yusuf's scent; God let him smell the scent clinging to the shirt from eight days' travel away according to Ibn Abbas, eighty parasangs according to Hasan and Ibn Jurayj, thirty days in another Hasan report, or ten nights in another.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r5.speaker: أبو أيوب الهروي
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r5.claim: Abu Ayyub al-Harawi reports that the wind asked permission to carry Yusuf's fragrance and God permitted it; Mujahid says the shirt's fragrance was from Paradise and reached Jacob, though Al-Alusi finds this attribution weaker than the direct link to Yusuf.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r6.claim: تفندون means to accuse someone of foolishness or corrupt judgment, especially senility; the word derives from fand, stone, as if the accused were made stone-like in understanding.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p53/r7.claim: Poetic lines use الفند for folly and rebuke; أفند الدهر فلانا means age ruined him, while مفند describes an old man whose judgment has failed.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p54/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p54/r1.speaker: الجوهري وغيره
ALUSI-FULL:v13p54/r1.claim: Al-Jawhari and other lexicographers say one calls an old man مفند, but not an old woman مفندة, since she supposedly had no judgment even in youth; al-Samin calls this odd, and Al-Alusi suggests women's intellect exists but declines with age.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p54/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p54/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p54/r2.claim: The جواب of لولا is omitted; possible completions are that his family would have believed him, or he would have said Joseph was near or would soon return.

ALUSI-FULL:v13p54/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v13p54/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v13p54/r3.claim: The addressees are identified either as the many sons who stayed behind when the others went to procure provisions, or as Jacob's grandchildren and relatives present with him; the latter is the common view.

ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r1.claim: Human knowledge cannot fully explain distant sensation or even ordinary perception; the verse permits such experiences without requiring a forced explanation, as knowledge remains limited.

ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r2.claim: The author recounts feeling sudden sorrow about his uncle at the moment of his death, then learning fifteen days later by letter that the uncle had died then and left him books.

ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r3.claim: He calls such distant impressions telepathy, groups them with inspiration, and says the same experience during sleep would be called a dream; they are common but not ordinary sources of knowledge.

ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r4.claim: Telepathic impressions range from ordinary delusion to levels of certainty that may reach the rank of a saintly wonder or miracle.

ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r5.claim: The verse's word rīḥ suggests conveyance; the author speculates that scent may travel through electrical waves and that scent itself may be a transferable force or vibration worth investigating scientifically.

ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:94-95#2/r6.claim: Even if a hidden law carries the scent, the event remains miraculous through God's control of its emission, extraordinary speed, and Yaqub's recognition; discovering a law does not erase the miracle.

ELMALILI:12:94-95/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:94-95/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:94-95/r1.claim: Yaqub asks his listeners to trust his senses and not call him senile, since they had already rejected even his earlier grief over Yusuf.

ELMALILI:12:94-95/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:94-95/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:94-95/r2.claim: The approaching caravan's news and Yusuf's fragrance bring Yaqub a spiritual foretaste of reunion and gradually prepare him for the joy to come.

ELMALILI:12:94-95/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:94-95/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:94-95/r4.claim: Commentators offer two explanations: God miraculously conveyed the scent into Yaqub's conscience or directly created it there.

ELMALILI:12:94-95/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:94-95/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:94-95/r5.claim: Current science can transmit sound electrically but, as the author observes, it does not yet know how to use electricity to transmit scent or smell.

ELMALILI:12:94-95/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:12:94-95/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:12:94-95/r6.claim: Yaqub's hearers resist believing him and treat his earlier longing as irrational, so he asks not to be dismissed as senile.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r1.claim: An omitted clause means the family set out and traveled with a caravan.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r2.claim: فصلت means moved away, as in Q 2:249; العير is the caravan that had arrived from Palestine.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r3.claim: Jacob's sensing Yusuf's scent is extraordinary inspiration and good news from God, recalling the shirt's scent; it is revelation without an angel, within Q 42:51.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r4.claim: ريح here means odor, a fragrance perceived by smell.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r5.claim: The emphatic wording anticipates denial; the omitted جواب لولا is “you would have confirmed it” if they did not accuse him of senility.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r6.claim: تفنيد means accusing someone of mental deficiency from old age; the first-person yā is dropped for ease while its kasra remains.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r7.claim: Those who accuse Jacob of old error are his household members present, not his sons, who were traveling; the referent is clear despite no prior mention.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v13p52#3/r8.claim: They mean Jacob persists in chasing an unattainable reunion; the metaphor casts him as off the path, and “old” reflects the 22-year separation, though their bluntness was culturally accepted.

TABATABAI:12:93-102/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:93-102/r2.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:12:93-102/r2.claim: Al-Majmaʿ reports that Jacob smelled Joseph from Palestine when the caravan left Egypt, at a distance of ten miles.

TABATABAI:12:93-102/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:93-102/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:93-102/r3.claim: Reports say Joseph's shirt came from Paradise, was worn by Abraham in the fire, passed through Isaac and Jacob, and was Joseph's amulet; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says they cannot be authenticated and their chains are weak.

TABATABAI:12:93-95/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:93-95/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:93-95/r4.claim: Faṣalat means the caravan departed and became separated; tufannidūn derives from fanad, weakness of judgment. Jacob senses Joseph's scent and expects their meeting soon, asking others not to dismiss him as foolish.

ASAD-NOTES:12:94#n94/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:94#n94/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:94#n94/r1.claim: The caravan had departed from Egypt.

ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.claim: Unlike Genesis' romantic account of Joseph's fortunes, the Qur'anic story illustrates God's unfathomable direction of human affairs: people may hate what is good for them or love what is bad for them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Faṣala means to depart; tafnīd means deeming someone foolish and therefore dismissing their opinion.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: A prophet's senses and faculties should not be compared to ours; even ordinary people can perceive more deeply in crisis, so Jacob detecting his son's scent is unsurprising.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:94/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:94/r1.speaker: some commentators
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:94/r1.claim: Some commentators explain Jacob’s distant perception of Joseph’s shirt as a miracle by which God carried its scent to him.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:94/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:94/r2.speaker: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:94/r2.claim: Elmalili calls the event an extraordinary divine transmission of scent and suggests it may inspire technology to capture and transmit scent, perhaps through electricity, though Jacob’s perception itself is miraculous.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:94/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:94/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:94/r3.claim: The author sees this as a multifaceted miracle demonstrating divine action, while allowing that natural laws related to it may exist; even recognizing a nearby person by scent would be extraordinary.

QIRAAT-ER:12:94:14#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:12:94:14#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:12:94:14#1/r1.claim: The standard form has kasra without the full yāʾ; the first-person yāʾ is elided in pause or standard recitation.

QIRAAT-ER:12:94:14#2/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:12:94:14#2/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:12:94:14#2/r1.claim: The variant retains the full first-person object-pronoun yāʾ with identical meaning.

STUDYQURAN:12:94/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:94/r1.speaker: My
STUDYQURAN:12:94/r1.claim: Jacob addressed the members of his tribe who were with him.

STUDYQURAN:12:94/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:94/r2.speaker: Bg and My
STUDYQURAN:12:94/r2.claim: Jacob sensed Joseph because the heavenly scent from Joseph’s shirt reached him as the caravan traveled from Egypt to Canaan.

STUDYQURAN:12:94/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:94/r3.speaker: My
STUDYQURAN:12:94/r3.claim: Some say Jacob’s perception was a miracle because both Jacob and Joseph were prophets.
